articles.title: Hurricane Lowell forecast: Category 3 storm nears Hawaii, prompting warnings
articles.summary: Hurricane Lowell is expected to pass to the west of the Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau. A hurricane warning is in effect for both, with a tropical storm warning for Oahu.
articles.body: Two of Hawaii’s islands are under hurricane warnings as Lowell, a Category 3 storm, nears. Lowell is expected to pass to the west of Kauai and Niihau late Monday and early Tuesday morning, according to the National Weather Service. A hurricane warning has been issued for both islands, with a tropical storm warning in effect for Oahu. “Preparations to protect life and property should be rushed to completion,” the NWS said. Kauai County Mayor Derek Kawakami urged residents to be off the roads by midday on Monday. He credited the Kauai emergency management team whose preparations put the county “in a good position to be able to weather this storm as one community.” “Hurricane Lowell is going to come a little closer than anticipated, and what that really means to everybody is that we are asking everyone to start sheltering in place,” Kawakami said. Residents who live in flood zones were advised to call friends and family members in safer areas to see if they would be able to house them. Officials referred people to refuge centers as a last resort. “I have to say, what I’ve observed over the last few days is nothing less than phenomenal,” Kawakami said. “I’ve seen people getting out there, getting prepared.” The island of Niihau, located less than 20 miles southwest of Kauai, does not have a mayor and is technically part of Kauai County. The worst of the storm is expected to occur overnight, but that could change, according to Kauai Emergency Management Administrator Elton Ushio. He warned of a threat of wind, water, flooding and storm surge. “Conditions are rapidly deteriorating,” Ushio said. “You know we’re having multiple rivers reaching flood stage. ... We could have a prolonged closure out there of the Kuhio Highway, but other areas island-wide could be affected.” Hurricane Lowell’s maximum sustained winds were recorded at 115 mph Monday morning local time, according to the NWS. The storm is expected to weaken on Tuesday, after moving by Kauai and Niihau. Storm surges of 2 to 4 feet are expected, as well as up to 16 inches of rain. The wet conditions on the island’s hills and mountains increase the risk of flash flooding and mudslides. There is also a possibility that the islands could see tornadoes form due to the high winds. Lowell previously reached Category 5 status but has since weakened. It’s the one of three cyclones that have swirled in the Pacific over the last week; the others are Hurricane Karina and Hurricane Marie, which brought rain and high surf to Southern California. This high level of storm activity in the Pacific is consistent with expectations for El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean. This year’s El Niño is forecast to be exceptionally intense, possibly record-breaking. Hawaii is still recovering from previous bouts of heavy rain and flooding after Tropical Storm Lala impacted the Big Island last month. At least one person died in a storm-related car crash and more than 100,000 people lost power. Just a week later, Tropical Storm Moke brought more rain. Now, as Lowell passes, some areas of Big Island could once again see up to 12 inches of rain, potentially compounding the prior storms’ effects. Hawaiian Airlines and Alaska Airlines said they planned to suspend flights in Lihue, Kauai’s only airport, as early as 11 a.m. local time on Monday. “We will reassess the forecast and airport conditions in Lihue this evening to determine plans to resume flights tomorrow,” the airlines said. “We are giving guests traveling to and from Lihue through tomorrow the flexibility to change or cancel their flights without fees.” United Airlines also said it would be monitoring the situation and offering waivers for customers looking to change their travel plans. The Kauai Emergency Management Agency urged residents to fill gas tanks, charge devices, refill prescriptions and gather water and food ahead of the storm. Residents should be prepared to stay home for several days, the agency said. The county’s department of water similarly recommended that residents stock up on drinking water and fill buckets and bathtubs for nondrinking use. Hawaii Gov. Josh Green announced that state and county offices in Kauai, including public schools, would be closed until Tuesday due to concerns about Lowell. He urged residents to follow guidance from local officials and remain indoors. “Closing offices, schools and courts will help keep people off the roads during dangerous conditions and allow emergency crews to focus on protecting our communities,” Green said. Residents began preparations as early as Wednesday, a manager of Kauai’s only Home Depot told NBC News affiliate KHNL. The station reported that the store was bought of out generators, tarps, and other emergency gear. Resident Nouveau Naumu told KHNL that he was 10 years old when Hawaii was hit by Hurricane Iniki. He remembered the devastation the 1992 storm left and was not taking Lowell lightly, he said. “I just remember the high winds, us kind of huddling in the bathroom and things were just hitting the house, all the debris, and then waking up the next morning you could see the devastation,” Naumu said.

articles.title: D4vd murder trial: Family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez calls for singer to face death penalty
articles.summary: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez is calling for the singer D4vd to face the death penalty after a Los Angeles judge ordered him to stand trial in the killing of the 14-year-old.
articles.body: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez is calling for the singer D4vd to face the death penalty after a Los Angeles judge ordered him to stand trial in the killing of the 14-year-old, whose dismembered remains were found in the trunk of his Tesla last year. “If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter,” the teen’s parents said in a statement Monday via their attorney. They released the statement on what would have been her 16th birthday. An attorney for the singer, whose real name is David Anthony Burke, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a separate statement, the family said they were “experiencing so many emotions” and “reliving unforgettable moments even though she is no longer here.” “These are feelings that only a father and mother and her siblings can share, with a heavy heart. We will always remember every moment and every good time we spent with Celestita,” the family said. The teen’s body was found in the front trunk of Burke’s Tesla at a Los Angeles impound lot in September 2025. Prosecutors said the car had been left on a street near Burke’s home and impounded at Hollywood Tow after someone reported an abandoned vehicle. A decomposed head and torso were found in a black cadaver bag, according to court documents, and a second bag contained additional dismembered body parts. Burke, 21, was arrested in April at a house on Marmont Avenue in the Hollywood Hills, Los Angeles police said. He has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains. At an evidentiary hearing in July, prosecutors said Burke began a relationship with Rivas Hernandez when she was 13 and ended it after she threatened to expose him. Text messages revealed in court showed that the teen had gotten pregnant by Burke and had an abortion. Last month, Burke abruptly parted ways with his legal team and asked to be represented by public defenders. An attorney for Rivas Hernandez’s family said in a statement that he does not deserve a public defender given his status and fame on social media. “The residents of Los Angeles County should be outraged because it will be the taxpayers that are picking up the tab to defend this millionaire,” attorney Patrick Steinfeld said. “David Anthony Burke is not indigent.”

articles.title: Russia’s quieter nuclear submarines threaten NATO, former commander warns
articles.summary: Russia's Yasen-M submarines and militarized Kola Peninsula are forcing NATO to confront a growing undersea threat across the GIUK Gap and Arctic, expert warns.
articles.body: Russia’s quieter new-generation nuclear-powered submarines are pressuring NATO’s northern defenses as the alliance races to secure Arctic and North Atlantic approaches to North America, a former NATO commander warned, citing President Vladimir Putin’s emerging "new super weapons and super capabilities" amassing in the region. The rising challenge, he said, also includes Russia’s heavily militarized Kola Peninsula, where Moscow has expanded military infrastructure, including airfields and ports, as it seeks to strengthen its position along the Northern Sea Route, as well as the waters leading to the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap, known as the GIUK Gap. NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum highlighted Sept. 2 that an expanding Russian submarine threat in the region was "serious." "Something is moving beneath the surface," NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum posted on X. ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW "Russia is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet. Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial capabilities into the High North," NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said. "They may be invisible beneath the waves. But not for us. We see them, we watch the developments closely and yes, we take these developments seriously," the Joint Force Command added. The combination of quieter nuclear submarines and Russia's growing military infrastructure across its Arctic coastline means NATO is confronting an increasingly difficult undersea surveillance challenge, retired Gen. Philip Breedlove told Fox News Digital. "Submarines are one of the toughest threats that we have to deal with — they're very hard to find and track," he explained. "Submarines can get well within striking distance of any nation in the Atlantic. From the United States to our NATO allies, submarines can get close enough to the shore to fire submarine-launched ballistic missiles and cruise missiles, which are a major problem," the former supreme allied commander Europe for NATO and commander of U.S. European Command added. REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES Today, countries such as Russia and China are developing similar fleets, posing a growing threat to any nation with a significant coastline, Breedlove said. "We've taken very capable measures in the past to understand what Russia is doing in those waters, and we will now be adapting to the possibility of a quieter submarine," he said. "Any increase in stealthiness or noise suppression by a Russian submarine is, of course, a problem for NATO." Russia's Yasen-M-class nuclear-powered submarines include advanced acoustic-quieting and sonar technology, according to Military Watch and Russian news agency, TASS. According to the U.S. Naval Institute, the 13,800-ton submarines can carry 1,000-mile-range cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles and hypersonic anti-ship cruise missiles, with Russian officials stating they remain "invisible." "Yasen-M-class nuclear-powered submarines are capable of accomplishing all of the Navy’s objectives in any part of the World Ocean while remaining invisible," Russian Navy Commander-in-Chief Fleet Adm. Alexander Moiseyev said in a June 17 statement, according to TASS, after Russia's Sevmash shipyard started building the ninth Yasen-M submarine. NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP "As is often the case when Putin is in trouble — and he's in trouble now in his war in Ukraine — one of the ways he diverts attention is to start announcing new super weapons and super capabilities that NATO and the West can't contend with," Breedlove warned. "Putin is creating a stir about a new class of submarines that he wants to deploy from what we call the bastion waters in the Far North," he said before stating that NATO would "have to adapt our measures and our ability to see and track them." "We've taken excellent measures in the past." Breedlove characterized the GIUK Gap as a critical gateway for Russian naval forces moving from their northern bases toward the Atlantic. "All the Russian ships have to come out through the GIUK Gap to make it into the Atlantic," Breedlove said, warning that the seven other Arctic nations, including the United States, are concerned about what Russia is doing. A UKRAINIAN HACKER'S TALE OF HOW HE IS AIDING THE LAND WAR BY BATTLING RUSSIA FOR THE CLOUD NATO has also been strengthening its northern posture amid the renewed Russian military activity and the growing strategic importance of the Arctic. In February 2026, the alliance launched Arctic Sentry, a multidomain military initiative led by Joint Force Command Norfolk and designed to better coordinate allied land, air and maritime activity across the Arctic and High North. NATO further strengthened its northern flank in June with Forward Land Forces Finland, a Swedish-led multinational force designed to bolster deterrence and defense along the alliance's northeastern flank, with Finland serving as the host nation, according to a release. "The Arctic region has been a concern for some years now as ice in the area is receding in the north, and what that has done is created the Northern Passage that allows European trade to happen with Asia much faster," Breedlove said, stating that for most types of ships, the trips are up to 14 days quicker. "This is a tremendous economic opportunity, but Russia sees this as an economic opportunity in that they want to control those northern waters. DENMARK VOWS TO DEFEND GREENLAND AFTER TRUMP REITERATES US SHOULD CONTROL TERRITORY Russia has been upgrading airfields, ports and radar systems along the Arctic coast as Moscow seeks greater control over the Northern Sea Route and its commercial traffic, Breedlove said. The recent NATO buildup however, has drawn strong pushback from Moscow, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov warning Aug. 30 that increased Western military activity risks destabilizing the Arctic region. articles.title: In 1876, Jesse James’s gang tried to rob a Minnesota bank for seven minutes; 150 years later the town still has a coat, a saddle and an outlaw’s mummified ear
articles.summary: US News: A seven-minute gun battle in a quiet Minnesota town helped bring down America’s most famous outlaw gang, leaving behind physical relics that are still.
articles.body: A seven-minute gun battle in a quiet Minnesota town helped bring down America’s most famous outlaw gang, leaving behind physical relics that are still preserved 150 years later. On 7 September 1876, the James-Younger Gang rode into Northfield, Minnesota, planning to rob the First National Bank. Instead of handing over their money, local residents fought back with pocketknives, rocks and hunting rifles. The failed raid lasted just seven minutes, leading to the largest manhunt in United States history at the time and effectively destroying the gang led by Jesse and Frank James. As reported by the Star Tribune in its Curious Minnesota series, the violent encounter left behind several historical items that are still kept in Northfield, including an outlaw’s duster coat, a leather saddle and the mummified ear of a dead gang member. The items are preserved and displayed by the Northfield Historical Society, which is located in the same building on Bridge Square where the First National Bank once operated.Seven minutes that ended an outlaw empireThe raid began shortly before 2:00 pm when eight heavily armed outlaws, including Jesse and Frank James and Cole, Bob and Jim Younger, entered Northfield. Three gang members went inside the bank while the other five watched the streets outside. Inside, acting cashier Joseph Lee Heywood refused to open the vault. He falsely told the robbers that a time lock protected the door. The gang members became angry as Heywood refused to give in. Outside, local residents realised a robbery was taking place and began firing from nearby shop windows and rooftops. Medical student Henry Wheeler shot and killed gang member Clell Miller from a second-floor window of the Dampier House hotel. Hardware store owner A.R. Manning shot Bill Stiles dead in the street. Inside the bank, one of the gang members shot and killed Heywood in frustration before the raiders escaped without any money. The entire gunfight lasted about seven minutes. "The James-Younger gang's foiled September 7, 1876 bank robbery took seven minutes, triggered the largest manhunt in US history up to that time and launched an enduring national industry in the enjoyment and study of outlawry," writer Karin Winegar noted in a historical commentary on the raid.Relics left behind after the battleSoon after the shooting, local residents collected equipment, weapons and personal belongings abandoned by the fleeing outlaws. Among the main items preserved in Northfield is a long duster coat left behind during the chaos. A heavy leather saddle was also abandoned by one of the gang members while fleeing south towards the Madelia swamps. The most unusual item is the mummified ear of gang member Charlie Pitts, who was killed two weeks later during a major shootout with a Minnesota posse in Madelia. After his death, medical workers preserved parts of his body, and his dried ear eventually became part of the historical collection documenting the end of the raid. The bank building itself is still largely intact. It includes the original vault door and a restored teller counter where Heywood made his final stand.A town that defeated the outlawsFrank and Jesse James managed to escape Minnesota and return to Missouri, but the rest of the gang was killed or captured. The Younger brothers, Cole, Bob and Jim, were all wounded and captured in Madelia. They later served long prison sentences at the Minnesota State Prison in Stillwater. The gang’s defeat became the defining event in Northfield’s history. Instead of hiding the violent episode, the town turned it into an annual community tradition. Every September, Northfield holds the Defeat of Jesse James Days, a festival that includes historical re-enactments of the seven-minute bank raid outside the original First National Bank building. The Northfield Historical Society continues to run the museum, attracting thousands of visitors each year who come to see the vault, the street corner where the gunfight took place and the physical relics left behind by the outlaws 150 years ago.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rwanda planted dozens of exotic tree species in an experimental forest in 1933; 90 years later scientists found eucalyptus had acidified the soil
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In Rwanda, an experiment with exotic trees grew into a much larger forestry programme, with eucalyptus eventually becoming the country’s dominant plan.
articles.body: In Rwanda, an experiment with exotic trees grew into a much larger forestry programme, with eucalyptus eventually becoming the country’s dominant plantation tree. A 200-hectare arboretum was established at Ruhande in Butare to test exotic species, including 63 species of eucalyptus, as Rwanda prepared to expand plantation forestry. By the early 1970s, eucalyptus plantations in Rwanda had reached about 23,000 hectares, part of a wider 95,684-hectare area across several East African countries. The expansion also brought questions about what intensive eucalyptus planting could mean for the environment. Researchers have examined concerns ranging from nutrient removal and soil quality to water use. According to the study published in Springer Nature Link, titled ‘Water use by short rotation Eucalyptus woodlots in southern Rwanda’, eucalyptus has been described as taking up large amounts of nutrients, potentially leaving soils poorer for other uses. However, the available research does not establish a 90-year soil-acidification finding at Ruhande, and the study discussed here focuses primarily on eucalyptus water use in southern Rwanda.Eucalyptus became Rwanda’s dominant plantation treeThe experiment was followed by a much wider expansion of eucalyptus planting. By the early 1970s, eucalyptus plantations across Ethiopia, Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya and Sudan covered 95,684 hectares, with Rwanda accounting for about 23,000 hectares at the time. The supplied paper notes that Rwanda and Ethiopia had the largest areas among those countries.In Rwanda itself, eucalyptus became the dominant plantation tree. The study states that eucalyptus accounted for 78% of forest plantations, with most plantations managed as short-rotation coppice. Small woodlots were particularly common, often appearing as groups or rows of trees scattered across farmland.Scientists raised concerns about eucalyptus and soilThe environmental effects of eucalyptus planting were already an area of scientific discussion. The supplied source notes that some researchers supported eucalyptus plantations for their economic, social and environmental benefits, while other research raised concerns about their effects on soil. In particular, it reports that eucalyptus had been described as taking up substantial quantities of nutrients, potentially leaving soils poorer for subsequent uses.The paper does not, however, report a 90-year comparison showing that eucalyptus at Ruhande acidified the soil. Its own research examined water use by short-rotation eucalyptus woodlots in southern Rwanda, rather than measuring a century-long change in soil acidity. The source cites a separate 2009 study titled Soil CO2 flux in six monospecific forest plantations in Southern Rwanda, but the supplied material does not provide that study's soil-pH results.Researchers measured eucalyptus water use in southern RwandaThe researchers examined eucalyptus woodlots in the Butare and Busoro catchments in southern Rwanda. The study found that the stands were generally small, frequently coppiced plantations, with tree diameters ranging from 2 to 36 centimetres. Potential tree transpiration ranged from 0.41 to 6.44 millimetres per day in the Busoro catchment and from 1.34 to 3.44 millimetres per day in the Butare catchment.The study's overall estimate was about 3 millimetres of potential tree transpiration per day, or roughly 1,095 millimetres per year. Long-term precipitation at the study site averaged 1,245 millimetres annually, and those dry-season water deficits could be reduced through lower leaf area and stomatal closure. The paper therefore concluded that the short-rotation woodlots studied did not necessarily produce a negative annual water balance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Huddersfield barrister jailed over revenge plot with client
articles.summary: Samreen Akhtar, 38, was jailed for three years and three months at Manchester Crown Court on Monday.
articles.body:
A barrister from West Yorkshire who plotted a revenge attack with her "career criminal" client has been jailed for more than three years.

Samreen Akhtar had represented Tabish Ali, who had been shot and injured in Blacker Road in Huddersfield on 14 September 2021.

The following day, the 38-year-old barrister, of Sufton Street, Huddersfield, was recorded on a telephone call to Ali putting forward a plan to find the person responsible for the shooting so they could be caused serious injuries, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Akhtar was convicted of encouraging or assisting the commission of an indictable offence, namely inflicting grievous bodily harm with intent.

At Manchester Crown Court on Monday, she was given a prison term of three years and three months.

Police said Ali was part of a drugs gang and was later charged with the murder of Jamal Nedd.

Nedd had been shot and killed outside his Huddersfield home as he was driving his mother to work on 19 December 2020.

Ali, of Clare Road, Cleckheaton, was charged with his murder in 2021 and later convicted and given a life sentence along with two other men in July 2022.

Their trial heard that the murder had come as part of an escalating "turf war" between drug dealing gangs and involving multiple violent firearms incidents.

The attempted murder shooting of Ali in 2021 was believed to have been linked to this ongoing feud, according to the force.

Akhtar denied the charge she faced but was convicted by a majority jury verdict following a five-day trial in June.

Det Insp Paul Hutchinson said: "As a professional working in the criminal justice system, Samreen Akhtar would have been acutely aware of her legal and moral responsibilities.

"But she chose to act outside of those to plot revenge with a dangerous criminal involved in a violent gang feud which included the brutal execution of a rival for which he was later convicted."

He continued: "In doing so, she became a criminal herself and showed a complete disregard for the standards that are expected of those in the legal profession."

articles.title: Govt clears Rs 1.1 lakh crore proposals to buy military hardware
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Rajnath Singh-led Defence Acquisition Council Monday gave in-principle approval (acceptance of necessity) for acquisition of military hardw.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Rajnath Singh-led Defence Acquisition Council Monday gave in-principle approval (acceptance of necessity) for acquisition of military hardware for the three services, including modernisation of fighter jets (Sukhois) and advanced light helicopters, purchase of chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear (CBRN) recce vehicles, radars, bridge systems and mine layers, at an estimated cost of Rs 1.10 lakh crore.A key feature of the defence approvals is the push towards domestic acquisition, reducing dependence on imports and giving a boost to govt's 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' initiative.On X, the defence minister said, "Of the total acceptance of necessity accorded, approximately 98% of procurements will be made from the Indian industry. It shows our commitment towards developing a strong defence industrial base in India."For Army, approval was granted for procurement of CBRN recce vehicles, high mobility vehicles (HMVs), self-propelled mechanical mine layers, advanced light helicopters (ALHs), trawl tanks and Sarvatra bridge system, the ministry said. While CBRN recce vehicles will be capable of detecting, identifying, monitoring and marking of areas contaminated with CBRN agents, trawl tanks are specialised military combat vehicles equipped with a front-mounted assembly designed to detonate landmines to clear a path from enemy mines.HMVs are expected to enhance operational capabilities, logistic support and mobility in challenging terrains. "The ALHs will execute complex missions across all terrains and operational situations for Army and IAF," it said.For Navy, approval was given for the procurement of Arudhra radars, design and development and subsequent procurement of marine gas turbines (MGT). Arudhra radars will replace the existing air route surveillance radars at various naval air stations, while MGT, a warship propulsion system, is expected to reduce dependency on foreign vendors.For IAF, approval was granted to various proposals to "enhance the war-fighting capability of fighters, transports and helicopters". Approval was accorded for procuring ground-based multi-purpose jammer and installing defence forces secure access card system, it said.

articles.title: Israel’s removal of Gaza rubble risk to war crimes evidence: UN
articles.summary: International Court of Justice ordered Israel in 2024 to prevent the destruction of evidence related to war crimes.
articles.body:
Israel’s clearance of rubble in Gaza could destroy evidence of war crimes, warns the United Nations.

States and companies removing the rubble “could incur international criminal responsibility” for destroying evidence of crimes committed during Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave, said the UN’s Special Rapporteur on the occupied territories, Francesca Albanese, on Monday.

It has been two years since the International Court of Justice ordered Israel to take effective measures to prevent the destruction of evidence relating to allegations under the Genocide Convention.

“It is unacceptable that the reconstruction of Gaza is conditioned upon the erasure of its past and the evidence required to secure justice for its victims”, said Albanese, a harsh critic of Israel.

The Israeli military carried out a massive operation in August to crush, mix and transport millions of tonnes of rubble from numerous sites, including cemeteries and other known locations of human remains.

A report by the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor issued last month said that the removal of debris from Gaza could be an attempt at demographic engineering and erasing evidence of the genocide.

Palestinian authorities estimate that more than 8,000 people remain buried under the debris, with many in Gaza still searching for the remains of loved ones. Israel continues to block the heavy machinery and forensic supplies needed to recover bodies.

On Sunday, Palestinians in northern Gaza held funeral ceremonies for about 100 people, including 60 children, whose remains were recovered from the rubble of destroyed buildings in Gaza City.

The head of Gaza’s civil defence service, Raed al-Dahshan, told Al Jazeera that with proper equipment, recovering remains from under the rubble could be completed in about 90 days, but it could take years without it.

articles.title: Palestinian parents fear for children's lives at school as settler attacks grow
articles.summary: A headteacher in the occupied West Bank has installed new barbed wire fencing after three pupils were killed this year.
articles.body:
On the first day of the new Palestinian school year, the head-teacher of al-Mughayyir boys school arrived at work before dawn, walking past the freshly installed barbed wire fencing and reinforced school gates as the sun began creeping through olive trees around the village, deep inside the occupied West Bank.

"We are scared," Bassam al Assaf told me. "The students are afraid, and their parents are afraid."

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

"I was inside my classroom and two little students came rushing to tell me there were settlers close to the school wall," remembers English teacher Waheed Abu Naem, whose brother Jihad was also killed by an Israeli soldier in the same attack.

Waheed said he was trying to move pupils to safety inside the school gate when the settler fired towards them. Mobile phone footage shows the moment Aws was shot.

"When I turned him onto his back, I saw lots of blood coming from his nose and mouth, and the bullet in his head," said Waheed. "We lost him."

He told me that bullets continued hitting the school building, as students hid behind the walls of their classrooms, or lay on the floor.

The Israeli military said in a statement at the time that stones had been hurled at a car carrying "civilians including a reservist soldier", and that the reservist had got out of the vehicle and fired at suspects.

Israeli media reported the reservist was later suspended from duty and an investigation launched.

Since that day, the casualties have grown alongside parents' fears.

Over the summer, two more pupils were shot dead by Israeli forces during settler attacks and incursions in the village, along with a 19-year-old who had just left the school.

In both cases, Israel's army said its forces responded to instigators of "a violent riot".

With three empty desks in the classrooms, some parents were reluctant to send their children back for the new school year.

The school sits right on the edge of Al-Mughayyir, an isolated village north-east of Ramallah, increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Bassam al-Assaf has installed a long barbed-wire fence around the compound and reinforced the school gates, to try and reassure parents. Ambulance crews are now stationed on the road outside, and several parents have volunteered to wait outside the school all day as an extra layer of protection.

BBC tracks one week of Israeli settler violence in occupied West Bank

Palestinian teens killed during settler attack on West Bank village

'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC

"I came because it makes the children feel their parents are with them, that they are safe, it gives them a kind of security," said Haroon Bishara, whose boys are in the first and second grades.

"We fear for our children more this year," he told me. "We know the situation is not safe at the school."

But he said that fear was mixed with a determination not to let the threat from settler attacks force them out.

Lined up in the playground for their first assembly, pupils heard the instructions repeated by teachers again and again throughout the day: if soldiers or settlers approach the school, don't shout, don't go near them, don't react.

Just over an hour after classes began, settlers were spotted through the school windows: two men, driving sheep through Palestinian fields a couple of hundred metres from the school, as Israeli soldiers stood close by.

Minutes later, another settler with a flock of sheep appeared.

"They have got closer to the village since April," said Abu Naem. They used to keep their sheep behind this [hill], but now the soldiers bring the settlers up to the village."

We asked the Israeli army for its response to all the allegations in this report, but they were unable to provide one before publication.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

But one of the ambulance crews stationed outside the school said that, rather than remove illegal settlements, Israeli soldiers had begun supporting and enabling settler incursions into the village.

Hadi al-Naasan, an ambulance driver in the village, said there had been a shift in the behaviour of Israeli forces over the past year. And that the rise in Palestinian deaths and injuries in al-Mughayyir this year reflected that.

"At the beginning of 2025, settler attacks were few, due to the army's interventions," he said. "In 2026, the situation changed completely: the settlers became fully protected by the occupation soldiers. This year, the number of martyrs is higher, the number of injuries is also much higher – and the number of child injuries is higher too."

Hadi, along with other residents of al-Mughayyir, believes that some Israeli settlers are now deliberately targeting children in order to put pressure on the adults in the village to leave their homes.

A UN Commission of Inquiry published in June found that settler attacks "have instrumentalized children as part of a broader coercive strategy to drive Palestinians off their land."

And it described "a pattern of settlers intentionally targeting Palestinian children" while they were playing near their homes, walking to and from school, tending to farms or herding livestock, "turning everyday spaces into sites of fear".

Israel dismissed the report as a "libellous sham".

Sheep farmer Sami Abu Rahma firmly believes that some violent settlers are targeting children.

At the end of July, his nine-year-old son Salim was shot and injured as he played with his siblings on the family sheep farm outside al-Mughayyir. The bullet is still lodged in his arm.

Footage from security cameras at the farm shows Salim pointing, and shouting to his parents that settlers are approaching, before running for shelter with his siblings and mother, as two gunshots are heard. Salim is seen grabbing his shoulder.

"In that moment, you stop thinking; you just feel fear," Sami told me. "Fear that, God forbid, [the attacker] was shooting to kill. The first thing in your mind is losing the most precious thing you have."

The man who shot his son, he said, lived in an illegal settler outpost that appeared next to the farm in June – and had previously shot at Salim in the same area a week before.

"You no longer feel you can keep them safe in the street, or even at school," he said. "The settlers don't want us to stay here, [they want us to feel] as if there's no future for us here."

Sami said he was the last sheep farmer left in the area, the others all chased away by settler attacks. The settler who shot his son had told the family repeatedly to leave their land, he said.

"No matter how determined you might be to stay," he added, "what do you do when settlers start shooting your kids?"

The regional settlers council told us that an off-duty soldier was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the shooting.

"We regret any harm to innocent people, Jews or Arabs, and oppose any act of violence that violates the law," it said in a statement, adding that it rejected "the attempt to attribute to the entire settlement community in Judea and Samaria acts that have not yet been determined by an investigation, as well as the baseless claim that lawful sheep grazing or Jewish presence in the area are part of a deliberate plan to harm children or drive residents from their homes."

Al-Mughayyir is part of a pattern unfolding across the occupied West Bank, with more illegal settler outposts encircling Palestinian villages, more protection for settlers from Israeli forces, and attacks moving from farms and grazing land to built-up areas, where women and children are more at risk.

"Children, seeing the army enter, don't grasp the gravity of the situation," said the local ambulance crew, Hadi al-Naasan. "Adults are more aware of how events can unfold."

UN figures suggest that the number of Palestinians injured during settler attacks by Israeli soldiers or settlers has risen sharply this year to an average of three injuries per day, and that the number of injuries inflicted directly by settlers themselves is also higher.

This rise has been accompanied by an expansion of Israeli settlements and settler outposts in the West Bank.

All Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law, and Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government is under growing international pressure - including from the UK, which is expected to announce sanctions this week in response to Israeli settlement policies.

The arrest of some violent settlers and a reported plan by Israel's prime minister to dismantle illegal outposts in the West Bank have not so far stopped attacks, nor reassured Palestinians who say outposts previously demolished by Israeli authorities were quickly rebuilt.

With Israeli elections less than two months away, Israel's Finance Ministry pushed forward plans this week to take over land registration in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, described by the Israeli settlement monitor Peace Now as "a clear step towards annexation".

Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has attributed settler violence to a tiny extremist minority, describing them in a recent television interview as "150 juvenile delinquents".

Since the beginning of 2025, the UN has recorded 316 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces or settlers, and more than 5,600 injured, to the end of July 2026. It says 20 Israelis were killed over the same period, including one child and eight members of the security forces, and 123 Israelis injured.

Palestinian parents who have stayed in villages like al-Mughayyir through escalating settler violence are now facing a growing fear of losing their children if they stay on their land.

articles.title: C-sections hit record high in Wales as mothers warn of support gap
articles.summary: Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support".
articles.body:
Mothers have described being left to recover from caesarean sections with "no support" as the number of babies being born via caesarean reaches its highest rate on record.

A caesarean, or C-section, is a major operation to deliver a baby through a cut made in a woman's stomach and womb.

Carys Louise Brandon, from Swansea, had an emergency C-section to deliver her first child in 2022 and said she was completely unprepared for what came afterwards.

Latest figures show 42% of babies in Wales were born by C-section in 2025, with just over half of those operations being emergencies.

The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to her needs.

After needing an emergency C-section, Carys, a content creator, said she had many unanswered questions about her recovery.

"I think I was thrown in at the deep end and I really didn't know how to deal with it," she said.

It was almost three weeks before the 29-year-old said she felt physically able to leave the house.

"And even then, I only walked up to the top of the street and back," she added.

Carys has since had two more caesareans and said each experience was very different.

Both times, she said the care she received in hospital and from her community midwife was good. But after getting home, she was left with questions about how her body should be recovering.

"You're thrown so into the deep end and there's no sort of, 'Oh, this is how your scar should look. This is quite normal for this sort of time'."

She recalled taking the dressing off her wound and fainting in the shower.

"I didn't know – should my scar be recovering in a certain way, should I really be feeling like this?

"There's just no support around the fact that after it, you're looking after a baby and recovering from major surgery, and everyone's recovery looks totally different."

She has shared her own experiences online in the hopes of helping other women, and said expectant mums often contact her for advice.

"I wish I'd had more stories that I could read to be a bit more informed before I gave birth that way."

The latest figures from the Welsh government showed that 42% of births in Wales were by caesarean section in 2025 – the highest rate on record - while in England around 45% of babies are delivered in this way.

According to the NHS , a caesarean may be recommended as a planned procedure or carried out in an emergency if a vaginal birth is considered to be too risky. Some women also choose to have a caesarean for non-medical reasons.

The health service's website states that most women can go home from hospital one or two days after a C-section, but that recovery is normally slower than from a vaginal birth.

A Welsh government report published in February highlighted the rapid increase in caesarean sections and inductions, saying the consequences for women, their families and the NHS had not been evaluated.

The report raised concerns about staffing and support across maternity services and said postnatal care was inadequately staffed and supported.

The Welsh government has committed to a three-year programme of improvements, but the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) said maternity services had not kept pace with the changing picture.

Julie Richards, director of the RCM in Wales, said postnatal care for C-sections should include support with pain relief, wound care and surgical recovery, alongside help with feeding and caring for a new baby.

She said the rise in caesareans had changed the demands being placed on services.

"What we may not have had is the developments in maternity care to respond to the change in landscape for maternity services."

Ceri Ann Roberts, 29, from Gwynedd, said the care she received at Ysbyty Gwynedd after giving birth to her second child last year had left her "traumatised".

Ceri Ann had an emergency C-section and her daughter, Ania, was taken to neonatal intensive care because she was not breathing.

Ceri Ann said she was then left alone on the recovery ward, unable to move.

"I just wanted to see my baby but I couldn't, and the staff told me there was no one available to take me up to see her."

She said it was seven hours until she held her baby for the first time, and that was when her husband arrived back at the hospital and took her to the unit himself.

"It was awful, I just cried and cried," she said.

Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board said while it could not comment on individual cases, women recovering from C-sections while their babies are in special care are supported by midwives who provide updates on their baby's wellbeing and help to facilitate visits to see their babies as soon as they are medically able to do so.

It acknowledged that being separated from a baby following birth could be distressing and said its teams worked to facilitate contact "at the earliest safe opportunity".

Nicola Rous-Morgan is a pregnancy and postnatal yoga teacher and a trained midwife, who works with women recovering after childbirth, including those who have had C-sections.

She said women often tell her they feel left alone to manage their recovery by themselves.

"I think one of the biggest take-homes is they felt that once they had been discharged from hospital, upon coming home, that they were just left to get on with it."

She added: "The focus is on women who are recovering from vaginal delivery. It's not geared towards women who are recovering from major abdominal surgery."

Nicola said women should not have to rely on private services or social media to find basic recovery information.

"These things shouldn't be things that women have to pay for privately. What happens to the women that can't afford that luxury?"

The RCM said staffing pressures were one factor affecting the care available.

Ms Richards said: "Our midwives are stretched, and quite often that is often impacted into the postnatal care, into the community settings."

The RCM surveyed its members in Wales in July, and 94% of respondents said they were not able to give the care they would like to give.

The organisation said midwives were working extra shifts and being moved to cover shortages elsewhere in maternity services.

Ms Richards said more investment and a workforce plan was needed.

The Welsh government said every woman should receive high-quality postnatal care tailored to their needs.

A spokesperson added: "Maternity teams provide postnatal assessment, advice and support following birth, and where required, women can be referred to specialist services including obstetric physiotherapy.

"Referrals are determined by individual clinical need to ensure women receive the most appropriate care to support their recovery and wellbeing."

"Recovery after birth matters, and where women tell us they have not felt listened to, supported or involved in decisions about their care, we expect services to learn from that feedback and act on it."

articles.title: A San Antonio library book checked out in 1943 travelled with one family for generations; 82 years later, it came back from Oregon with a note about the late fee
articles.summary: US News: Some library books disappear for a few months. Others never make it back. But one copy of Your Child, His Family, and Friends took nearly 82 years to .
articles.body: Some library books disappear for a few months. Others never make it back. But one copy of Your Child, His Family, and Friends took nearly 82 years to complete its journey home. According to the San Antonio Public Library, which announced the unusual return in August 2025, the book was checked out in July 1943 and was due back 28 days later. The story was also reported by Texas Public Radio and CBS News. Instead, it resurfaced in June 2025, arriving at the library from Oregon with a letter explaining how it had spent more than eight decades away.A book that travelled across generationsThe book, written by Frances Bruce Strain, was found among the belongings of the sender’s late father in Oregon. The person who returned it believes their grandmother had originally borrowed the book when their father was 11 years old. At the time, the family was preparing to relocate to Mexico City, where the grandmother was transferred for work with the U.S. Embassy.The book appears to have travelled with the family, eventually making its way through the generations before landing in the hands of the Oregon resident who discovered it. Rather than keep the decades-old library copy, the person decided it was time to send it back to San Antonio.The return came with one slightly awkward questionAlong with the book was a handwritten letter that included a lighthearted concern: whether the family would still have to pay the overdue charge. It was a reasonable question, considering the book’s original checkout date.A notation inside the book showed that the library’s fine at the time was three cents per day for keeping a book beyond its due date. Had that rate simply been applied across the entire period, the amount would have approached $900. But the returning family got lucky, at least as far as the library’s current rules are concerned.The late fee is no longer a problemThe San Antonio Public Library eliminated overdue fines in 2021, saying the move was intended to reduce financial barriers to using its services. So there was no decades-old bill waiting for the book when it finally arrived home.There is also an important wrinkle to the potential calculation: library officials noted that under historical policies, an item could eventually have been treated as lost and charged at its replacement cost, meaning there is no definitive figure for what the actual bill would have been. Either way, the book escaped a very expensive reunion.From a 1943 checkout to a ibrary displayThe returned copy was reportedly still in good condition despite its extraordinary journey. For a short time, the book was put on display in the lobby of San Antonio’s Central Library, turning an ordinary parenting book from the 1940s into a small piece of local library history.After the display, the library planned to donate it to the Friends of the San Antonio Public Library, which would offer it for sale through the Book Cellar used bookstore. Proceeds from the store support the library. More than eight decades after it was borrowed, the book’s story has become almost as interesting as the one printed on its pages, a reminder that sometimes a library book doesn’t simply get returned. It becomes part of a family’s history before finding its way home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Glasgow Life charity buys Third Eye centre and CCA archive
articles.summary: Exhibition records, photographs, films, posters, flyers and artists' letters chart the story of two organisations that were central to Glasgow's art scene.
articles.body:
The charity that manages Glasgow's museum and library collections has bought the archive of two organisations that played a key role in the city's contemporary art scene.

The collections of the Third Eye Centre and the Centre for Contemporary Arts (CCA), containing material gathered over more than 50 years, are now owned by Glasgow Life.

Items include exhibition records, photographs, films, posters, flyers and artists' letters, providing a record of the people and work that helped establish Glasgow as a centre for contemporary art.

The acquisition follows the closure of the CCA and the sale of its Sauchiehall Street building and assets.

The CCA building in Sauchiehall Street was originally home to the Third Eye Centre, which was established by the Scottish Art Council in the 1970s.

With performers including Billy Connolly, Whoopi Goldberg and American poet Allen Ginsberg, a key figure in the Beat movement, the venue was an outlet for Glasgow's counter culture.

It closed in 1991 with the CCA taking its place as a hub for the city's art scene.

The venue endured a turbulent time in recent years, having been first forced to close in 2018 after a fire destroyed the nearby Glasgow School of Art.

Several of the businesses which rented out space inside the building never returned after it reopened.

The centre's popular cafe bar - the Saramago - closed permanently in 2023 after a lengthy and bitter dispute over staffing issues led the venue to discontinue its relationship with the bar - a decision that resulted in a financial hit.

The CCA itself temporarily closed in December 2024 , saying this was in a bid to secure its long-term future amid significant financial concerns.

But earlier this year the venue was permanently closed and all staff were made redundant.

Glasgow Life worked with Creative Scotland and The Ballast Trust to acquire the collection, with funding provided by Creative Scotland.

The archive will now be catalogued by Glasgow Life's City Archives team before being made available to researchers, artists, students and the public.

Jane Rowlands, Glasgow Life's head of museums and collections, said the archive was an important part of the city's cultural history.

She said: "The Third Eye Centre and CCA helped shape Glasgow's reputation as a place for creativity and contemporary art.

"Securing this archive means an important part of that story will remain in Glasgow, where it can be cared for and made available to future generations."

Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan said she was pleased the archive had been kept in public ownership and would remain accessible.

by a Hindu religious group linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS), as reported by Euronews.The iconic Paris landmark's operator, SETE, said the closure was due to representative, told French TV that female workers had been "moved away from their workstations as the delegation passed by" during the group's visit on Saturday.Eiffel Tower employees condemned what normal opening hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others," it said."To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower," it continued, adding that it articles.summary: Georgetown University students promoted a Charlie Kirk lookalike contest on Fizz, the anonymous social media app, drawing over 2,200 upvotes on campus.
articles.body: Students at Georgetown University are allegedly planning a Charlie Kirk "lookalike contest" for the anniversary of the conservative activist’s assassination, with the event drawing thousands of upvotes at the elite Washington, D.C., campus, according to screenshots shared with Fox News Digital from the school’s Turning Point USA chapter. The Sept. 10 event was promoted on Fizz, an anonymous social media platform popular with Georgetown students, where the initial announcement received more than 2,200 upvotes. Georgetown's undergraduate population is roughly 6,000. The post that received 2,200 upvotes read, "Charlie Kirk lookalike contest. September 10th 2026. Pull up to Copley Lawn to speak the truth while the cost is high." INSIDE CHARLIE KIRK’S EFFORT TO DEVELOP THE NEXT GENERATION OF CONSERVATIVE VOICES Georgetown's TPUSA chapter said members believe the slogan "pull up to Copley Lawn and speak the truth while the cost is high" is likely a mocking statement. Copley Lawn is an area right outside the school's most iconic landmark, Healy Hall, which resembles a castle. The Turning Point USA chapter responded by setting up a table on campus with American flags, stickers and signs condemning the planned event, according to the group. TEXAS MAN ALLEGEDLY THREATENED TO BOMB TURNING POINT USA EVENT AND KILL CEO ERIKA KIRK IN ONLINE POSTS According to posts on the Fizz app, there has also been an Erika Kirk look-alike contest discussed, with someone commenting, "Can the winner of the Charlie Kirk one be prom king with the winner of this?" The group says that they are not sure who started the calls for the lookalike contest, but believe it was first brought up on Fizz, which they say is the most popular anonymous platform used by Georgetown students. According to the group, users must be affiliated with Georgetown University in order to log into Georgetown's Fizz as it requires a "@georgetown.edu" email address. One Fizz user appeared to suggest The Georgetown Chimes, a choral group at the school, sing a Charlie Kirk meme song, "We Are Charlie Kirk" writing, "Any chance Gtown Chimes could learn this before Thursday?" HASAN PIKER SINGS MOCKING 'WE ARE CHARLIE KIRK' SONG AT LIVE PODCAST SHOW The song, thought to be AI-generated, was released shortly after Kirk's assassination in Utah. Another post, shared on the Georgetown Fizz account, read, "Happy Kirkiversary, September 10th, on Healy Lawn," and included what appeared to be an AI-generated image of Kirk, and included the phrases, "Georgetown University," "Honoring leadership, inspiring truth," and "Charlie Kirk lookalike contest." This reaction from Georgetown students should disturb us regardless of our political affiliation. There is a difference between disagreeing with someone’s politics and celebrating their death." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Andrew Kolvet, TPUSA's spokesman said, "A culture that can no longer simply mourn the fallen, or respect them enough to at least keep their mouth shut, is a culture that has lost touch with a basic sense of shared humanity. We take these anonymous posts seriously and condemn their language as deeply inconsistent with Georgetown University’s values. We are monitoring this closely to ensure the safety of the University community." The spokesperson continued, "Georgetown is committed to ensuring that all members of our community have a safe and welcoming place to learn and receive the support they need to do so. We seek to create a living and learning community that promotes thoughtful, respectful dialogue." articles.title: Food price cap plans giving farmer 'sleepless nights'
articles.summary: East Lothian farmer Jamie Wyllie says he's worried costs will get passed down the line to the food producers.
articles.body:
As a farmer, Jamie Wyllie is used to getting by on little sleep. His job requires long hours and hard graft.

But now he said something else is keeping him up at night – the prospect of the Scottish government introducing price caps for some essential food items.

Ministers say that the big supermarket chains will take the financial hit, insisting "bold action" is needed to help households.

But Wyllie's fear is that the costs will get passed down the production chain, and ultimately come to rest with his family farm which is making "little to no margin as it is".

Wyllie is an office holder in the National Union of Farmers in Scotland, so is in regular contact with fellow farmers.

And they're not the only interested parties who have expressed concerns.

Just last week 23 organisations wrote to the first minister to call on him to ditch the policy.

Business groups urge Swinney to scrap 'ineffective' food price cap plan

Swinney's 100-day push gives way to bigger battles ahead

How much should we be prepared to pay for our food?

So what exactly is the Scottish government proposing?

They want to see a price cap implemented for up to 50 essential items, such as milk, eggs, cheese and rice.

Large supermarkets would be expected to offer at least one variety of these items at a capped cost.

If they sold out of that, they could then be required to offer another similar product at the same price.

John Swinney has previously said he has a "public health responsibility" to ensure that people can afford a healthy basket of goods.

And he's well aware that many families are struggling with the basics due to cost of living increases.

Beyond the four staple items the first minister has identified, we don't know what food products he has in mind.

And we don't know what prices they would potentially be capped at.

The policy is currently out for consultation, allowing interested parties to give their views.

The idea is that the big supermarkets would be the ones carrying the financial burden of the policy.

Speaking on his East Lothian farm, Wyllie said that - in reality - that's probably not how things will play out. He fears the big retailers will pass any losses down to producers like him.

He said: "I struggle to see how, or why, they would swallow that cost"

"They'll pass it down to us. We see it all the time".

And he worries that when the supply chain dust settles, it will be him that picks up the bill.

"I'm the bottom of the food chain. I can't pass my costs on to anybody else," he added.

He runs a number of farms, specialising in pigs, sheep and crops for bread and cereal production and his costs have increased in recent years.

There's been a UK government national insurance hike and there's a looming UK-wide tax on fertiliser that will affect a farm of his size.

On top of this, his energy costs have doubled in recent years, with a standing charge of £1,500 per month before he's even used a single unit of electricity.

Jamie worries that a food price cap could prove to be another burden that "might make producers think twice about what they're doing".

When asked what he means by that, he points out that farmers have other potential options: from switching to non-food crops, to selling their land so that AI data centres can be built on them.

He said that independent farmers are already spread thinly, doing every job from bookkeeping, to HR, to tractor driving.

He said: "Every time other items get thrown in, like this price cap, it does affect you. It does keep you up at night".

On Tuesday, the Scottish government will host a 'fair food summit'.

Business Minister Tom Arthur will meet with organisations representing producers and retailers.

Ministers have made it clear that they want to engage with all those involved in the supply chain, and address any concerns they may have.

The invite for this event said that the idea is to "work together to ensure that people across Scotland can afford their weekly shop in a way that works."

But it seems that a number of producers don't see a way to achieve all the objectives.

They seem to think you either cap prices or protect producers. There's scepticism that both can be done in tandem.

But John Swinney has made it clear that the cost of living remains a top priority for him. And he sounds determined to see the policy become a reality, though there's speculation that there could be legal hurdles down the line.

But he's not the only politician who has been exploring this area. The UK government has also asked retailers to freeze some prices , though it has stopped short of forcing shops to do so.

Whatever comes out of Tuesday's summit, ministers are planning to push on with plans for price caps.

Within the detail of an impact assessment published by the Scottish government last week there were options being floated that could water it down slightly, including prices still being allowed to rise but tracking below rates of food inflation.

When Swinney outlined this policy during May's Holyrood election campaign, it was definitely one of the most eye-catching proposals on offer from any party.

No one could accuse him of not proposing bold ideas to address a key concern that voters have.

But it also could prove to be incredibly complicated to deliver.

And ministers will have their work cut out convincing farmers like Wyllie that it can come to fruition without hitting his bottom line.

articles.title: Flight recorders recovered from 'devastating' Amazon cargo plane crash
articles.summary: Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300 overshot the runway at Miami International Airport.
articles.body:
Investigators have recovered the flight recorders from the Amazon cargo plane that crashed at Miami International Airport, but the priority remains the recovery of victims, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has said.

Five people were killed and five others seriously injured when the Boeing 767-300, operated by 21 Air, overshot the runway shortly before 14:00 local time (19:00 BST) on Sunday.

The plane hit two vehicles, including a white van carrying seven people within the airport perimeter, and a Toyota with three passengers.

NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said it was too early to draw conclusions about what caused the crash, with investigators still in the "fact finding stage".

Speaking at a press conference at Miami International Airport on Monday, Homendy said the aircraft had two crew members on board and was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, on its third flight of the day.

The plane struck navigational aids and equipment after overrunning the runway, before hitting a white Ford van owned by a contract cleaning company.

It then travelled through a perimeter fence and collided with a Toyota Corolla , coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

Homendy described the crash scene as "devastating", with debris from the aircraft, vehicles and airport fencing scattered across the area.

"It's hard to see, and I'm sure very difficult for the first responders as well," she said.

She said recovering victims' bodies was the current priority, adding: "The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait."

The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered and are being sent to NTSB headquarters for evaluation.

Homendy said investigators could not yet say anything substantive about the cause of the crash as they were still collecting evidence at the scene.

Investigators will examine the flight history, crew experience and training, radar data, and aircraft performance. Separate teams will look at the plane's systems and engines, while a meteorologist will assess the weather conditions at the time of landing.

The NTSB will also examine whether the runway should have had an engineered materials arresting system (EMAS), which is designed to slow and stop aircraft that overrun a runway. Homendy said this would be a "key" part of the investigation.

Earlier analysis by BBC Verify found there was an active thunderstorm near the airport shortly before the crash, with winds gusting up to 26 knots.

The NTSB has appealed for members of the public to share photographs or videos that could aid the investigation.

Homendy said the agency would make safety recommendations at the end of its investigation. "That's why we're here - to prevent the next tragedy," she said.

"Our recommendations must be implemented, or we'll be here again."

Two of the four runways at the airport remained closed following the crash . Passengers have been warned to expect further disruption after Sunday's cancellations affected the arrival of aircraft and flight crews.

The crash happened during the Labor Day holiday weekend, one of the busiest travel periods in the US.

Amazon said it was "heartbroken" by the loss of life and that it was working closely with authorities.

21 Air, the company operating the aircraft, expressed its condolences and said it was co-operating with the investigation.

articles.body: The five people killed when an Amazon-branded cargo plane overran a runway in Miami on Sunday had been inside a van that was transporting a cleaning crew and an SUV outside the airport, the National Transportation Safety Board said Monday. Five others were injured in the incident at Miami International Airport. NTSB chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said at a news conference that the aircraft struck a white Ford van owned by Professional Ocean Service Corporation, a contract cleaning company for airlines, which was inside the airport. Seven people were in the van, she added, but did not comment further about the injuries or deaths. After that, the plane hit a Toyota SUV that had been driving outside the airport, Homendy said. She said the primary focus is on the “recovery of the victims.” “The investigation and access to the aircraft, as well as evidence, can wait while that goes forward,” Homendy told reporters. She described the scene of the crash as “devastating” and said the van had been “torn apart.” “You can see on the paved surface tire marks that continue through the grass. There’s debris everywhere,” she said. “The SUV, you can see airbags, the surrounding airbags. You can see components from vehicles, both passenger vehicles and the aircraft itself.” The Boeing 767-300 aircraft overran the runway during a landing, officials said. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel previously said that the flight was operated by 21 Air. “We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport. Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss,” Nantel said in a statement. 21 Air CEO Keith Winters said in a message on its website that it is cooperating with federal investigators and offered condolences to the victims’ families. Two crew members were onboard the aircraft at the time of the crash, Homendy said. Miami-Dade Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said Sunday that the pilot and co-pilot had initially been trapped inside the plane. A cellphone video obtained by NBC South Florida shows a crew member jumping out of the plane after the crash. A photo sent to NBC News, meanwhile, shows one of the crew members being taken away on a gurney at the airport. The plane had come from San Juan, Puerto Rico and had completed two prior flights on Sunday, Homendy said. It went from Cincinnati, Ohio, to Miami, and then Miami to San Juan before the crash. Upon landing back in Miami, the aircraft overran the runway and struck navigational aids and equipment, according to Homendy. The plane then hit the Ford van, traveled through a perimeter fence, and struck the Toyota SUV, which was traveling on Northwest 67th Avenue, she said. The aircraft continued into the grass where it hit a fence line, which separated an area where Tesla robo-taxis were stationed, Homendy said. She added that investigators still have to be “somewhat cautious” as they probe the causes of the crash because of safety concerns on the scene. “There’s fuel everywhere that will have to be remediated,” she said. Homendy said it was too early to release much information about the factors that contributed to the disaster, as the investigation has just begun, though she suggested more details could become available on Tuesday. The plane’s flight data and cockpit voice recorder have been recovered, she said, and the NTSB will look at air traffic control and aircraft performance as it probes the crash. The agency’s investigators expect to be on scene for at least a week, she said, and asked the public to send in photos or videos that are relevant to the investigation.

articles.title: Hawaii braces for Hurricane Lowell
articles.summary: Threats of cyclones and deadly surf as the Category 3 storm path approaches Hawaiian islands on Monday night.
articles.body:
Hurricane Lowell, a major Category 3 storm in the Pacific Ocean, has crept closer to the Hawaiian islands with forecasters warning the weather systems could unleash tornadoes on the islands of Kauai and Niihau.

On Sunday, the United States National Hurricane Center issued emergency hurricane and tropical storm warnings for the island chain, advising residents and visitors to brace for severe windstorms and possible mudslides as early as Monday night local time. Lowell is predicted to skirt just west of Hawaii’s most northwest main islands, Niihau and Kauai, as well as portions of the vast Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument, tracking from south to north.

Mayor Derek Kawakami of Kauai issued an emergency proclamation in anticipation of the hurricane.

Kauai faces potential coastal flooding of up to 1 metre (3 feet) caused by rolling storm surges and unusually high tides.

The storm has been gradually pivoting toward the more rural islands in the Aloha state, moving north at 9 km/h (6 mph), according to the hurricane center. Lowell started as a tropical depression that formed over the Pacific Ocean on August 27. It was driven by a combination of warm ocean temperatures and an active El Nino pattern.

Lowell has seesawed between Category 3 and Category 5 intensity as its trajectory mushroomed. It first reached Category 5 intensity at 257 km/h (160 mph) on Wednesday morning local time, becoming the second Category 5 hurricane of the season. Only two other Pacific hurricanes in recorded history have regrouped to a Category 5 after losing strength mid-path: Emilia (1994) and Ioke (2006).

Ioke was the strongest ever recorded in the central Pacific, while the island of Kauai sustained billions in damage during Hurricane Inike, a 1992 Category 4 storm and the largest recorded in Hawaii’s history. Six people were killed.

Forecasters said Lowell could bring rainfall of 150mm to 250mm (6 to 10 inches), with maximum totals of 360mm (14 inches).

Lowell had maximum sustained winds of 195km/h (120 mph) and was pinpointed about 895km (about 555 miles) southwest of the state capital, Honolulu.

Local officials have been urging residents and visitors to prepare for a downpour of rain and fierce winds which could cause major flash flooding and hazardous mudslides.

According to the National Weather Service, tornadoes could accompany tropical cyclones. They typically occur in rain bands well away from the center of the storm.

Hawaii’s Big Island can expect as much as 100mm to 200mm (4 inches to 8 inches) of rain, with localized peaks reaching up to 305mm (12 inches).

Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 85km (50 miles) from the centre while tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 280km (175 miles).

Kauai’s Emergency Management Agency urged residents to fill gas tanks, charge devices, refill prescriptions and store water and food ahead of the storm. The agency also said residents should be prepared to stay home for several days.

Swells generated from Lowell are expected to produce “life-threatening surf and rip current conditions”, according to a statement by the Kauai County government on Sunday evening. It urged visitors to stay out of the ocean and steer clear of the shoreline as coastal conditions rapidly worsen.

“Residents should not assume conditions will be limited to areas near the storm’s center,” the government said.

As panic-buying emptied supermarket shelves in Lihue on Kauai, residents of the 8,000-person airport town scrambled to stock up on food and water.

Real estate agent Lori Benkert bought an extra 4.5kg (10 pound) container of propane so that she could cook on the barbecue if power shut off. Benkert manages dozens of properties on Kauai and has boarded up two houses on the western side of the island.

“We’ll lose some power, probably have some trees, a bunch of tree limbs coming down,” Benkert told The Associated Press. “Everybody is probably going just to hunker down”.

Meanwhile, Category 1 Hurricane Marie churned 1,120km (695 miles) south-southwest of San Diego in southern California, bringing dangerous surf to the area and Mexico’s Baja coast. Packing 120km/h (75mph) sustained winds, the storm tracked northwest at 11km/h (7mph).

Even without coastal watches or warnings, updrafts from Marie will hit southwest Mexico, Baja California and Southern California over the next few days, creating pounding surf and dangerous rip currents.

The islands of Hawaii rarely experience tornadoes, averaging about one per year. Just 42 tornadoes were reported in the state between 1950 to 2018, according to Stephen Parker, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Honolulu.
